questions.statement: Sofia wrote less carefully, so Andres's essay is ______?
questions.context: A teacher in Alajuela compares two students who wrote the same essay.

options.feedback: Correct! The comparative of 'good' is the irregular form 'better', so it needs no 'more' at all.
'Best' is the superlative, which would rank his essay against all the others, not only against Sofia's.
No English word 'goodest' exists: the irregular series is only good, better and best.
'More good' is not used, because 'good' is irregular and never takes the intensifier 'more'.

questions.explanation:
Good, bad, well, badly and little are irregular adjectives and adverbs. They form comparisons with better, worse, less and least, never with more or the suffixes -er and -est.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Of the five runners in the club, Daniela is ______?
questions.context: A coach in Puntarenas talks about the runners in her club.

options.feedback: 'More' builds the comparative of a long adjective, so it can never stand in front of the short adjective 'fast'.
'The most' marks a superlative, but 'fast' has one syllable and takes the suffix -est instead of 'most'.
Correct! A superlative among more than two items takes 'the' plus the -est form: the fastest of the five runners.
'The most' and the suffix -est are two separate systems, and combining them counts the degree of comparison twice.

questions.explanation:
One-syllable adjectives build the superlative with -est and always take 'the'. 'Most' is reserved for adjectives of three syllables or more, such as 'the most comfortable bus'.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Kevin and Daniel got the same grade, so their essays are ______ quality?
questions.context: Two students from Heredia compare their scores on the same exam.

options.feedback: 'Than' introduces a real difference, so it cannot appear inside the frame that marks two equal qualities.
Correct! Equality of two things is built with the fixed pair 'as + adjective + as' and no 'than' at all.
'As much' goes with measured nouns such as 'money', not with the adjective 'good', which needs the bare form.
'So ... as' expresses equality only in negative clauses, as in 'not so good as', never on its own.

questions.explanation:
Equality between two things uses the frame 'as + adjective + as'. Its negative form keeps both 'as' words: 'not as good as'. 'Than' can never appear inside that frame.

questions.statement: Which sentence corrects the mistake in "Her bike is more cheaper than mine"?
questions.context: A student in Cartago is correcting a sentence in the school magazine.

options.text: Her bike is cheaper of mine.
options.feedback: The frame 'of' belongs to the superlative 'the cheapest of the group', and it needs the article and a group.

options.text: Her bike is more cheap than mine.
options.feedback: 'More' is used with long adjectives, so it cannot join the short adjective 'cheap', which builds its -er form alone.

options.text: Her bike is the cheaper than mine.
options.feedback: A comparative cannot be introduced by 'the'; only the superlative 'the cheapest of ...' is shaped that way.

options.text: Her bike is cheaper than mine.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Cheap' is a short adjective, so it takes the suffix -er and 'than'; 'more cheaper' applies two systems at once.

questions.explanation:
Never mix the two comparison systems: short adjectives take -er and -est, while long adjectives take more and most. 'More cheaper' applies both at once, so it counts the comparison twice.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: By bus she arrives ______ than by car, so she leaves home an hour earlier?
questions.context: A commuter in Heredia compares how she and her brother travel to work.

options.feedback: Correct! 'Early' turned into an adverb of manner, and the comparative of that adverb is 'earlier', not 'more early'.
'More early' treats the adverb as a long adjective, but 'early' keeps the short pattern and needs the -er form.
'Earliest' is the superlative, so it would need 'the' plus a group, while this sentence compares only two options.
'The earliest' is a superlative form, and a superlative can never be linked to 'than', which marks a difference of two.

questions.explanation:
Manner adverbs usually follow the adjective pattern: early becomes earlier and earliest, hard becomes harder. Such a comparative then compares two people, actions or ways of doing something.

questions.statement: The more she trains, ______ she runs in the morning?
questions.context: A coach in Liberia trains young runners on a mountain track.

options.feedback: The base form cannot open the second half; the correlative pair requires the comparative form 'faster' there.
Correct! The double comparative repeats the structure: 'the more + clause, the + comparative + clause'.
The form is right, but the pair needs 'the' before it in the second half just as it does in the first.
'The fastest' is a superlative, which would rank her against every runner in the country, not two habits.

questions.explanation:
The double comparative has two matched halves: 'the more + clause, the + comparative + clause'. Each half repeats 'the' and takes a comparative form, never the base or the superlative.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: This blue cloth is ______ than that one, so it costs far more?
questions.context: A tailor in Escazu compares two pieces of cloth for a school uniform.

options.feedback: 'A little' weakens the degree of a difference, but the adjective must still keep its -er form: 'a little cheaper'.
Only 'slightly' can stand in front of a comparative, and 'slight' without the ending cannot modify one at all.
'Many' counts separate plural items such as buttons, so it cannot measure the degree of an adjective comparison.
Correct! 'Much' measures a large degree, and 'expensive' is a long adjective that needs 'more' before the base form.

questions.explanation:
Intensifiers change the degree of a comparison, never its form. 'Much' and 'far' raise it, 'a bit' and 'slightly' lower it, and the adjective keeps the same -er or more form.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: After the storm, the trail to Cerro Verde was ______ than the main road?
questions.context: A hiker in Monteverde compares two trails after a rainy week.

options.feedback: Correct! A consonant plus 'y' changes to 'i' plus '-ier' in the comparative, so 'muddy' becomes 'muddier'.
'Mud' is a noun in this sentence, so it cannot carry a comparative; the adjective 'muddy' is what needs the form.
'Muddiest' is a superlative and cannot be linked to 'than', which only ever introduces a comparison of two.
'The muddiest' would need a group of named trails, and ending it with 'than' contradicts the superlative it already is.

questions.explanation:
Spelling rules decide the shape of longer adjectives. A consonant plus 'y' turns into 'i' plus '-er', as in 'muddier', and 'easy' becomes 'easier' before 'than'.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She is one of the ______ students in the whole exchange program?
questions.context: A university guide in San Jose introduces exchange students to her class.

options.feedback: 'Of' can only follow a superlative that already carries 'the', as in 'the tallest of the group', and never follows 'one of'.
'Much' measures the degree of a single comparative such as 'much better', but 'one of the' needs a superlative instead.
Correct! After 'one of the' comes 'most' and a plural noun: 'one of the most hard-working students' in the program.
The article would be doubled, because 'one of the' has already supplied it: 'one of the the most' is impossible.

questions.explanation:
'One of the' plus a superlative names a single member of a wider group, so the noun must be plural: 'one of the most talented students'. A second 'of' cannot follow.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The teacher said it was ______ of the two posters she received?
questions.context: A teacher in Heredia shows two final projects to her class.

options.feedback: 'The best' is a superlative, which needs a group wider than the two posters lying on her desk in front of the class.
Correct! A pair is compared with the comparative plus 'of the two': the better of the two posters she received.
'More' never combines with 'good', and in any case a pair of items is handled by the comparative, not by 'more'.
'Most' cannot modify a two-syllable adjective, and the phrase 'the most good' is not accepted English at all.

questions.explanation:
English keeps the comparative for a pair and reserves the superlative for three or more. So among two posters we say 'the better of the two', while among all of them we say 'the best'.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: This year's coffee harvest is ______ last year's: 12 tons against 4 tons?
questions.context: A coffee farmer in Grecia compares two harvests for an international buyer.

options.feedback: 'Bigger than' adds a second comparison on top of the ratio, so the sentence would claim far more than the tonnage shows.
'Times more than' multiplies twice by implication; English uses 'times as ... as' when it wants to state an exact ratio.
Correct! 'Tons' is uncountable, so the base form is repeated inside the equality frame: three times as much as.
A bare 'the' introduces a superlative with one winner, and 'times of' has no second item to compare with here.

questions.explanation:
Ratios are built by repeating the base form inside the equality frame: twice as much as, three times as long as. The base form stays unchanged because the numbers already state the multiplication.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She paid ______ for the bus to SJO as her cousin did for hers?
questions.context: A student in Liberia compares what she paid for a bus ticket with her cousin's.

options.feedback: Correct! Money is measured with 'much' inside the equality frame, so 'as much as' is the pairing that fits here.
'Far' measures distance or length, so 'as far as' belongs to a journey and not to an amount that was paid.
'Many' counts separate plural items such as tickets, while the sum of money in this sentence cannot be counted.
'Long' measures time or length, so it cannot describe the price of a bus ticket in any comparison.

questions.explanation:
The noun after the second 'as' tells you which measure word fits: money takes much, distance takes far, countable items take many, and time or length takes long.

questions.statement: Which sentence uses the superlative of place with the correct structure?
questions.context: A tour guide in La Fortaleca describes a beach to her group of visitors.

options.text: It is the most crowded beach of the country.
options.feedback: After a superlative a location takes 'in', because 'of' would require a named group of items and not a place.

options.text: It is the most crowd of the beaches in the country.
options.feedback: 'Crowd' is a noun, so 'most' cannot modify it; the superlative has to be built from the adjective 'crowded'.

options.text: It is most crowded beach in the country.
options.feedback: Dropping 'the' removes the comparison itself, since only the definite form claims that this beach ranks above the rest.

options.text: It is the most crowded beach in the country.
options.feedback: Correct! 'In' names the place where the group is found, and the definite article comes before the superlative in the country.

questions.explanation:
Superlatives about places use 'in' plus a location, as in 'the busiest street in town', while 'of' plus a group names the members being compared, as in 'the busiest of the three streets'.

questions.statement: The college enrolled ______ students than last year, so classes are smaller?
questions.context: A librarian in San Jose compares enrollment numbers between two academic years.

options.feedback: 'Less than' compares an amount that cannot be counted, but students are counted one by one in both cohorts.
Correct! Students is a countable plural noun, so its comparative is 'fewer than' rather than 'less than'.
'Many' counts plural items and cannot measure the degree of a comparison the way 'far fewer' or 'much fewer' does.
'The fewest' is the superlative, and it would need a group wider than the two cohorts of students named here.

questions.explanation:
Countable plurals take fewer in the comparative and the fewest in the superlative; uncountable nouns take less and the least. The choice depends on whether the noun can be counted.

questions.statement: Which brochure sentence uses comparison structures with no error at all?
questions.context: A senior student proofreads a brochure for a study abroad office.

options.text: Her semester in Canada was the more exciting than the one in Spain.
options.feedback: A comparative cannot be introduced by 'the', and 'more exciting than' is already complete, so both elements are wrong.

options.text: The course in Quebec is cheaper and the most demanding than ours.
options.feedback: Only one half can be comparative: 'cheaper' works, but 'the most demanding' is a superlative and rejects 'than'.

options.text: Her semester in Canada was far more exciting than the one in Spain.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Far' measures the degree of a long comparative, and 'than' is the only marker 'more exciting' needs.

options.text: The Quebec course is the cheapest of the two than the local program.
options.feedback: The frame 'the cheapest of the two' already compares the options, so adding 'than' duplicates the comparison marker.

questions.explanation:
Each comparison frame is exclusive. A comparative joins with than and no article, a superlative needs the plus in or of, and a pair is handled by the comparative of the two.

questions.statement: Rewrite as a two-way comparison: "This is the fastest route to Alajuela"?
questions.context: A teacher in San Jose asks her students to rewrite one sentence for a test.

options.text: This route is the faster than the one to Alajuela.
options.feedback: The article 'the' belongs to the superlative, so it must disappear once the sentence turns into a comparison of two.

options.text: This route is more fast than that to Alajuela.
options.feedback: 'Fast' is a short adjective, so it takes the -er form rather than 'more', and 'that' cannot stand after 'than' alone.

options.text: This route is as fast than the one to Alajuela.
options.feedback: Equality uses the double 'as' frame, which replaces 'than' completely instead of combining with it in one sentence.

options.text: This route is faster than the one to Alajuela.
options.feedback: Correct! Two routes are compared, so 'the fastest' becomes 'faster than' and the article drops away.

questions.explanation:
Converting a superlative into a comparative means three changes at once: drop 'the', replace the -est form by the -er form, and introduce the second item with 'than'. All three must happen together.

questions.statement: Her second result is ______ than the first one, though both are normal?
questions.context: A lab technician in San Jose compares two blood test results on the same machine.

options.feedback: 'Not as high' leaves the comparison unfinished, because the clause still needs the closing 'as' and the second term.
Correct! Negated equality keeps both halves of the pair: not as high as, with one 'as' on each side of the adjective.
'No higher than' works with countable nouns such as 'no higher than ten', but a measured test value takes the 'as' frame.
The word 'as' cannot be stranded at the end, since the pair 'as ... as' always keeps one 'as' on each side of the adjective.

questions.explanation:
The negative equality frame 'not as + adjective + as' mirrors the positive one, so both 'as' words remain even when the comparison is cancelled. Deleting either one leaves a broken clause.

questions.statement: Which order shows the comparatives from the weakest to the strongest degree?
questions.context: A language teacher in Tibas writes degrees of comparison on the board.

options.text: much bigger, far bigger, slightly bigger, a bit bigger
options.feedback: The order jumps from 'much' to 'far' and then falls back to the weakest modifiers, so the rising scale is broken in the middle.

options.text: a bit bigger, much bigger, slightly bigger, far bigger
options.feedback: Placing 'much' before 'slightly' breaks the rising order, and 'far' has to stay at the strongest end of the scale.

options.text: slightly bigger, a bit bigger, much bigger, far bigger
options.feedback: Correct! Intensity rises from slightly to a bit, then to much and finally to far, so the list reads from weak to strong.

options.text: far bigger, slightly bigger, a bit bigger, much bigger
options.feedback: Starting with 'far' reverses the request, because the question asks for the weakest degree before the strongest one.

questions.explanation:
Comparative modifiers form a graded scale: slightly and a bit are weak, much is strong, and far is usually the strongest. The adjective keeps the same -er form in every position.

questions.statement: Which sentence about the three runners contains no comparison error?
questions.context: A coach reviews three athletes' times before the national meet in Alajuela.

options.text: Karl's time is better than Pedro's, and Ana ran the fastest of the three.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Better than' is the irregular comparative of 'good' for two runners, and 'the fastest of the three' uses the superlative group correctly.

options.text: Karl's time is more better than Pedro's, and Ana ran the fastest of the three.
options.feedback: 'Better' is already comparative, so adding 'more' creates the double form 'more better', which is never correct.

options.text: Karl's time is better than Pedro's, and Ana ran the most fast of the three.
options.feedback: 'Fast' has one syllable, so it takes the suffix -est in the superlative 'the fastest' and never the intensifier 'most'.

options.text: Karl's time is the better than Pedro's, and Ana ran the fastest of the three.
options.feedback: A comparison of two cannot be introduced by 'the', which belongs only to the superlative of a wider group of runners.

questions.explanation:
Two decisions control every comparison: how many items are involved, and which form the adjective takes. Mixing irregular forms with 'more' or 'most' breaks the pattern.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She wants to warn that the two options are very different. Which sentence says that?
questions.context: A senior writes an email to a university advisor in San Jose.

options.text: Option A is the most better than option B.
options.feedback: 'Better' is already comparative, so 'the most better' stacks two systems and cannot be used to measure a wide degree.

options.text: Option A is more well than option B.
options.feedback: 'More' does not combine with the irregular 'well', whose comparative is 'better'; 'more' would require a long adjective.

options.text: Option A is better than option B.
options.feedback: This sentence reports a difference but adds no degree modifier, so the warning about a clear gap between the options is lost.

options.text: Option A is far better than option B.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Far' adds a wide degree to the comparative, so the sentence signals a clear difference between the two options.

questions.explanation:
Choosing a degree modifier is part of choosing a comparison. A bare 'better than' only reports a difference, while 'far', 'much' or 'even' tells the reader how wide that difference is.
